world_behind.title: Four years, and a complete cycle
world_behind.text: Sixth year: no wars, but grief. Seventh: three thousand five hundred baptized and continual peace. Eighth: the same church waxing proud. Ninth: the chief judge resigning. Twenty verses carry the record from mourning to revival to corruption to reform, the shape the whole book will keep using.

world_behind.title: The revival is caused by loss
world_behind.text: Verses 2 and 3 tally what the wars of the previous two chapters took: the dead, the livestock, the ruined harvest. Then they report that the survivors believed this was the judgment of God upon them. The belief is what wakes them, and the record gives it as their own reading of events rather than as its verdict.

world_behind.title: The pride list is an inventory, and the industry is credited
world_behind.text: Verse 6 names exceeding riches, fine silks, fine-twined linen, flocks and herds, gold, silver, all manner of precious things, and adds "which they had obtained by their industry." The chapter does not say the wealth was stolen or unearned. It says what was done with it.

world_behind.title: A growth report, and the numbers go the wrong way
world_behind.text: Verse 9 has the church's pride exceeding the pride of everyone outside it. Verse 10 reports that the congregation itself had become the obstacle for outsiders, and that its growth stopped. This is an institution auditing its own effect on people who never joined.

world_behind.title: Two men named Alma, and the verse has to say so
world_behind.text: Verse 4 has people baptized "by the hand of Alma, who had been consecrated the high priest over the people of the church, by the hand of his father Alma." The elder died in the last verse of Mosiah. The sentence exists to fix which one is standing in the water and where his authority came from.

world_behind.title: The transfer is legal, and it uses the machinery
world_behind.text: Verse 16 runs the appointment through the voice of the people, with the new man's powers spelled out: lawmaking bounded by the code already on the books, and enforcement. Two chapters ago that instrument produced a civil war; here it seats a chief judge without incident.

world_behind.title: The two offices finally come apart
world_behind.text: Mosiah 29:42 put the judgment-seat and the high priesthood on the same man in the same sentence. This chapter separates them, and Alma keeps the one with no power of enforcement attached.

words.text: Set apart to an office by a formal act. Treated at 2 Nephi 1:7. The chapter uses it twice and both are about handing authority along: Alma made high priest by the hand of his father, and teachers, priests and elders made by Alma. Two verses later the people so ordained are the ones grieving over what their congregation has become.

To grow, to become. Treated at 2 Nephi 7:9. It is an intransitive verb about change over time. "Wax proud" appears once in scripture. The verb matters because it is gradual: nobody in verse 6 decides to be proud, and the eighth year arrives with the same people in it who were baptized in the seventh.

Full of contempt, treating another as beneath notice. It turns up once here and three times in the Old Testament, always of a posture rather than an act. The verse pairs it with persecution of those who did not believe according to their own will and pleasure. Contempt first, then pressure.

Something set in a path that makes a person fall. The figure appears five times in this record and never once in the Bible; everywhere else the thing in the road is a doctrine or a scripture people cannot get past. Here it is a congregation. What trips the outsiders is not what the church teaches but how the people who already hold it behave.

Bringing low, putting down, and here it is reflexive and voluntary. Others were "abasing themselves." The word appears once in this record and once in the New Testament, and both times somebody is doing it to himself. It is the exact opposite motion from "lifting themselves up" three words earlier in the previous verse.

Running to help, from a root meaning to run beneath, to get under a load. The participle is unique in scripture, and the verse doubles it: succoring those who stood in need of their succor. Help is defined by the need.

Skill bent to deception. Treated at Mosiah 7:21. Alma sets out to pull down, by the word of God, all the pride and craftiness and all the contentions among his people. The record uses the noun five times; the Bible uses it five more, mostly of arguments made in bad faith. It is the vice of the capable.

phrases.term: They were awakened to a remembrance of their duty
phrases.text: The formula for how this record thinks repentance usually starts. Not a new conviction but a remembered obligation. The verse before it lists what they lost. The losing is what causes the remembering, and the chapter will spend its second half showing how short that kind of memory runs.

phrases.term: There was continual peace in all that time
phrases.text: The chapter's one untroubled sentence, and it is attached to a membership figure: about three thousand five hundred baptized in the seventh year. This is the third time in a dozen chapters that the record has reported continual peace: after the reform, after Nehor, and here. Each time the sentence stands just before a collapse.

phrases.term: Which they had obtained by their industry
phrases.text: Six words that keep the chapter honest. The wealth is earned. Whatever goes wrong in the eighth year is not a story about theft or luck, and the clause is inserted in the middle of the indictment.

phrases.term: Even to exceed the pride of those who did not belong
phrases.text: The comparison the chapter is willing to make. The measure is whether the church is worse than the people around it, and on this reading it is. The sentence ranks the church below the people outside it.

phrases.term: From one piece of iniquity to another
phrases.text: Example as an active force, with a direction and a rate. The words describe a sequence, and the verse ends by naming where the sequence goes: the destruction of the people. A congregation is being told that its ordinary conduct is a public instrument.

phrases.term: He saw great inequality among the people
phrases.text: The word Mosiah used when he abolished the monarchy, in the mouth of the man he handed the country to. The verse spells out what it looks like from the ground: some lifted up with pride, despising others, turning their backs on the needy, the naked, the hungry, the athirst, the sick.

phrases.term: Nevertheless the Spirit of the Lord did not fail him
phrases.text: A clause placed against "began to be very sorrowful" in the same sentence. The record does not resolve the sorrow or explain it away; it puts one fact next to the other and moves on. The verb "fail" is the same one used of the church five verses earlier.

phrases.term: Bearing down in pure testimony against them
phrases.text: The method, named after every other method has been ruled out. The verse says he saw no way to reclaim them save this. "Pure testimony" appears once in scripture, and the whole of Alma 5 through 16 is what the phrase turns into.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: A conversion figure given to the nearest round number
verses.text: The record supplies a count: "about three thousand five hundred souls that united themselves to the church of God and were baptized." Numbers of this kind are rare in these books, which usually report growth as multitudes or as the whole land. The hedge "about" is kept, and the figure is fixed to a single year, the seventh of the judges. It can be set against the census-style claims elsewhere, such as the twenty-three units of ten thousand at Mormon 6:10–15, as an example of the record counting when it chooses to.

verses.label: v. 9–10
verses.title: A comparison stated as a measurement
verses.text: The record does not say the church members were proud. It says their pride ran higher than the outsiders', "even to exceed the pride of those who did not belong to the church of God." Verse 10 draws the practical consequence in the same comparative terms, that their wickedness "was a great stumbling-block to those who did not belong to the church." Two verses in a row rank the inside against the outside and both times the inside comes off worse, which is an unusual direction for a record kept by the church's own high priest.

verses.label: v. 16–18
verses.title: An office split in two, with the mechanism named
verses.text: The record separates powers explicitly and reports how the appointment was made: a wise man was given power "according to the voice of the people," which is the procedure established at Mosiah 29:26. Verse 17 supplies the name, Nephihah, and verse 18 states the division without ambiguity: "Alma did not grant unto him the office of being high priest over the church, but he retained the office of high priest unto himself; but he delivered the judgment-seat unto Nephihah." Two offices, held together for eight years, are separated in a single verse.

verses.label: v. 19–20
verses.title: A resignation with its reason stated as a last resort
verses.text: The record supplies the motive rather than leaving it to be inferred: he stepped down so that he might "pull down, by the word of God, all the pride and craftiness and all the contentions," and the clause that follows makes it a judgment about available means, "seeing no way that he might reclaim them save it were in bearing down in pure testimony against them." A man who has just given away the power to enact and enforce laws says in the same passage that laws will not fix the problem.

chapter.title: The whole cycle runs inside twenty verses
chapter.text: Affliction, humility, revival, prosperity, pride, decline, reform. The record usually spreads this over a book. Here it is compressed to four dated years, which makes the shape visible in a way the long versions never quite are.

chapter.title: What produced the revival was loss, and the revival did not hold
chapter.text: Three thousand five hundred people were baptized in the seventh year; the eighth year has the church out-priding the world. The chapter puts the number and the collapse two verses apart and declines to comment on the arrangement.

chapter.title: The church becomes the obstacle it was meant to remove
chapter.text: Verse 10 is the hardest sentence in the chapter: the wickedness of the church was a stumbling-block to those who did not belong to it. The people outside are not described as hostile. They are described as tripped.

chapter.title: Two congregations under one roof
chapter.text: Verse 12 has people despising others and turning their backs on the needy. Verses 13 and 14 have people abasing themselves and succoring the same needy. Both are in the same church in the same year, and the record refuses to average them into a single verdict.

chapter.title: Mosiah's word comes back on Mosiah's country
chapter.text: He built a government to end inequality and named it in the founding document. Nine years later the man he handed the country to looks at it and uses the same noun. A constitution can distribute power and still leave this untouched.

chapter.title: The diagnosis is that the law cannot reach it
chapter.text: Alma holds the highest judicial office in the country and gives it up, because nothing on the statute books addresses scorn, or backs turned on the hungry, or a congregation whose example is leading outsiders downward. Verse 19 says he saw no way save testimony.

chapter.title: The handover is orderly, voluntary, and partial
chapter.text: Four steps are recorded in three verses: selection, "he selected a wise man who was among the elders of the church"; confirmation, "according to the voice of the people"; the powers granted, "to enact laws according to the laws which had been given, and to put them in force"; and the reservation, "Alma did not grant unto him the office of being high priest." Alma 2:1–9 has the same voice of the people rejecting Amlici, whose faction then "did consecrate Amlici to be their king." The machinery that failed two chapters earlier is here reported working.

chapter.title: Role in the book
chapter.text: Alma 4 is the hinge of the whole volume. Up to here the book of Alma is political history; from verse 20 onward it is preaching, and the next twelve chapters are sermons. The theory behind the decision gets stated much later, when the record says the word had more powerful effect on the people than the sword.

applications.title: Check what your prosperity is doing to your attention
applications.text: The wealth was earned by industry and the record says so. What changed was where they were looking. Earning something honestly is no protection against what having it does to you.

applications.title: Measure yourself against the people outside
applications.text: The chapter's indictment is comparative: the church's pride exceeded the pride of those who did not belong to it. Progress against your own worst year can hide the fact that you are now behind the room.

applications.title: Ask who is tripping over you
applications.text: The people harmed here never joined. Before defending your conduct on its own terms, work out what it looks like to someone standing outside deciding whether to come in.

applications.title: Notice both halves before you judge the whole
applications.text: The same church in the same year contained people turning their backs on the hungry and people running to feed them. Institutions are rarely one thing, and describing them as one thing is usually a way of avoiding somebody.

applications.title: Let the need define the help
applications.text: The verse measures the assistance by what was lacking, and it says so by repeating the same root twice in four words.

applications.title: Give up the lever that does not work
applications.text: He had legal power over these people and concluded it could not reach the problem, so he handed it to someone competent and went to do the thing that could. Keeping authority you cannot use with the problem in front of you is its own kind of vanity.

applications.title: Hand it on properly
applications.text: He chose a wise man, specified the powers, ran it through the voice of the people, and named him. A resignation done well is an appointment.

questions.text: What woke me up last, and was it a loss?
What have I earned honestly that is quietly changing what I look at?
If I were ranked against people who make no claim to my convictions, where would I come out?
Who has decided against something good because of how I behaved?
Whose need am I meeting on my own schedule rather than theirs?
What am I still holding that cannot fix what is actually wrong?
